title: THE KING HAD THE CROWN—BUT GOD PUT THE MESSAGE IN HULDAH’S MOUTH
paragraphs: THE KING HAD THE CROWN—BUT GOD PUT THE MESSAGE IN HULDAH’S MOUTH

When Josiah’s officials needed to know what God was saying, they walked past power, position, and prestige and went to a prophetess in Jerusalem. What she told them was terrifying. What happened next reveals something every believer desperately needs to remember: when the Word of God exposes you, the condition of your heart determines what happens next.
There are moments when God does not whisper what we want to hear.
He tells us what we need to hear.
And sometimes the person carrying that truth is someone we never would have expected.
King Josiah had a problem.
Not a political problem.
Not a financial problem.
Not an enemy gathering outside Jerusalem's walls.
Something far more dangerous had happened.
The Word of God had been found.
Think about the tragedy hidden inside that sentence.
The temple was still standing.
Priests were still serving.
Religious activity still existed.
Yet the Book of the Law had become so neglected that its discovery became an event.
You can have a temple and lose the Word.
You can preserve religious activity and lose obedience.

You can know Christian vocabulary, attend church, post Bible verses, sing worship songs, wear a cross around your neck—and still discover that somewhere along the way the living Word of God stopped governing the hidden rooms of your life.
That is where Josiah's story becomes uncomfortable.
During repairs to the temple, Hilkiah the high priest found the Book of the Law and gave it to Shaphan the secretary. Shaphan read it, then carried it before the king.
And when Josiah heard what was written, he tore his clothes.
He did not argue with Scripture.
He did not edit Scripture.
He did not accuse Scripture of being too severe.
He did not search for someone who would reinterpret God's commands until his disobedience felt comfortable.
The king broke.
That may be one of the most important details in the entire story.
Because God's Word had exposed a scandal much bigger than Josiah himself.
Judah had forsaken the LORD.
Generations had wandered.
Idolatry had penetrated the nation.
Judgment was no longer an abstract theological concept. Josiah realized that his people stood guilty before a holy God.
So he commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah to inquire of the LORD.
And then Scripture gives us a detail too important to rush past.
These powerful royal officials went to a woman named Huldah.
The Hebrew text identifies her as:
חֻלְדָּה הַנְּבִיאָה
Ḥuldāh han-nevī'āh.
Huldah the prophetess.
The word הַנְּבִיאָה — han-nevī'āh is the feminine form identifying her as a prophetess.
This was not a title modern readers placed upon her.
This is how the biblical text presents her.

Huldah was the wife of Shallum, who was associated with the royal wardrobe, and she lived in Jerusalem's Second Quarter. When the king's delegation needed an authoritative prophetic response concerning the rediscovered Book of the Law, they went to her. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 34 preserves the same essential episode.
Pause there.
The king had the crown.
Hilkiah had the priesthood.
Shaphan had access to the palace.
But Huldah had been entrusted with a word from God.
And when these men arrived, she did not flatter them.
She did not appear intimidated by their titles.
She did not ask what message would be most acceptable to the king.
She spoke.
Her declaration begins with the unmistakable prophetic formula:
כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה
Koh amar YHWH.
“Thus says the LORD.”
Those words change everything.
Because Huldah was not offering a motivational opinion.
She was delivering a divine indictment.
Judah had forsaken God and turned toward other gods. The consequences announced in the covenant were coming upon them.
Imagine standing in that room.
These men represented the king.
One softened sentence could have protected Huldah socially.
One convenient reinterpretation could have made everyone more comfortable.
Instead, she delivered the message faithfully.
God's judgment was coming.
That is something Christianity cannot erase without eventually erasing the Cross itself.
We love saying God is love.
And He is.
We love saying God forgives.
And He does.
We love talking about grace.
We should.
But grace becomes sentimental nonsense if there is no real sin from which we need saving.
The Cross is not proof that sin does not matter.
The Cross is proof of how terribly sin matters—and how unimaginably far God's saving love was willing to go.
Huldah's message reminds us that the God of Scripture is holy.
Idolatry matters.
Rebellion matters.
Forsaking God matters.
The things we secretly worship matter.
And idols do not always have statues anymore.
Sometimes an idol fits inside your pocket.
Sometimes it looks like approval.
Sometimes it sounds like applause.
Sometimes it is money.
Sometimes it is lust.
Sometimes it is bitterness you refuse to surrender because hatred has begun feeling safer than forgiveness.
Sometimes it is a relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ.
Sometimes it is ministry itself—when being seen serving Jesus becomes more important than actually knowing Jesus.
Sometimes the idol staring back at us from the throne is ourselves.
That is why Huldah's story cannot remain an interesting account about an ancient prophetess.
The Book has been opened again.
And now it is reading us.
But Huldah's message did not end with judgment.
There was another message specifically for Josiah.
And this is where the story becomes painfully beautiful.
God said that because Josiah's heart was tender and because he humbled himself when he heard God's words—because he tore his clothes and wept before God—the LORD had heard him.
One Hebrew expression in 2 Kings 22:19 is especially striking:
יַעַן רַךְ־לְבָבְךָ
ya'an rakh-levavkha.
“Because your heart was tender…”
A tender heart.
Not a perfect résumé.
Not flawless ancestry.
Not political power.
A heart that could still be pierced by the Word of God.
That may be the question following you through this article.
Is your heart still tender enough for God to correct you?
Not, “Do you go to church?”
Not, “Do you believe Christian doctrine?”
Not, “Do people think you are spiritual?”
Can God's Word still break through your defenses?
When Scripture confronts something you love that God calls sin, what happens inside you?
Do you surrender?
Or negotiate?
Do you repent?
Or rationalize?
Do you weep?
Some of us have become frighteningly skilled at hearing sermons without hearing God.
We know when to say amen.
We know which worship songs make us emotional.
We know how to appear spiritually alive.
But when Scripture touches the one room we have locked…
the secret addiction…
the hidden messages…
the resentment…
the dishonesty…
the pornography…
the pride…
the relationship we have placed above Christ…
the unforgiveness we have rehearsed for years…
suddenly we become theologians looking for loopholes.
Josiah did something radically different.
He tore his clothes.
In his culture, that outward act expressed profound grief and distress.
But God looked deeper than torn fabric.
God saw the heart underneath it.
“Your heart was tender.”
There it is again.
That sentence should haunt us in the best possible way.
Because perhaps the greatest spiritual danger is not discovering that you have sinned.
The greater danger is reaching the point where discovering your sin no longer bothers you.
When conviction disappears, we should not automatically congratulate ourselves for finding peace.
Sometimes peace is surrender to God.
Sometimes what we call peace is simply a conscience we have repeatedly trained ourselves to ignore.
Josiah heard the Word and trembled.
And God heard Josiah.
What an extraordinary exchange.
Josiah heard God.
God heard Josiah.
This is where the road begins turning toward the Gospel.
Because Josiah's humility mattered, but Josiah could not ultimately carry Judah's guilt away.
His reforms were significant, but he was not the final Savior.
Another King had to come.
A greater Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
Josiah tore his garments because he heard judgment.
Jesus would allow His own body to be torn as He bore our sins on the Cross.
Josiah humbled himself before the Word of God.
Jesus, though without sin, humbled Himself in obedience to the Father, even unto death.
Josiah's reforms could confront idols.
Jesus came to transform idol-making hearts.
And at Calvary, judgment and mercy met in a way Huldah's generation could only anticipate within the unfolding story of redemption.
Jesus did not come to tell sinners that rebellion never mattered.
He came because it mattered eternally.
The Gospel is not God shrugging at your sin.
The Gospel is the holy God doing what you could never do to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
Grace does not mean God pretends the scandal never happened.
Grace means Jesus can rewrite what the scandal was going to become.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean repentance magically erases every wound we caused.
It means sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Shame does not have to write it.
Addiction does not have to write it.
Your past does not have to write it.
The worst thing you have ever done does not possess sovereign authority over the rest of your story.
Jesus does.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere beneath the polished Christian version of yourself there is something you are exhausted from hiding.
You have smiled while breaking.
Served while struggling.
Prayed publicly while privately wondering how you wandered this far.
Perhaps you are afraid that if people really knew what happened, they would look at you differently.
Perhaps they would.
But Jesus already knows.
He knows the chapter you keep trying to tear out.
He knows what happened behind the closed door.
He knows what you searched.
What you said.
What you touched.
What you took.
Who you hurt.
What you concealed.
He knows.
And still the Gospel calls you to come into the light.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Christ is sufficient.
Repentance is not God's attempt to humiliate you.
It is His call to stop running toward death.
The same Word that exposes our rebellion points us toward the Savior.
So perhaps your response today should resemble Josiah's—not necessarily torn clothing, but a torn-open heart.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary.
No pretending.
Just:
“Jesus, I have sinned. Have mercy on me. Change me. I don't want to keep hiding.”
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Your honesty may become somebody else's courage.
Your testimony may remind a stranger that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend slowly drifting from Christ.
The believer hiding an addiction.
The person carrying unbearable shame.
The Christian who still attends church but whose heart has quietly grown cold.
There may come a night when you need to remember that conviction is not the end of the story.
There may come a morning when somebody you love finally admits, “I need help.”
Come back to this.
Send it to them.
Sit beside them.
Pray with them.
Point them to Jesus.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase your sins.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
Supporting Gospel work should flow from gratitude and willing generosity—not fear, pressure, or the idea that God owes us something because we gave.
That distinction matters.
Huldah did not manipulate the king.
She delivered God's Word.
Josiah did not bargain with God.
He humbled himself.
And the Gospel does not invite us to manipulate God either.
It invites us to repent and believe.
So before you leave this article, imagine that ancient scene one more time.
A king waits in Jerusalem.
Five officials stand before a prophetess.
A forgotten Book has been opened.
A nation has been exposed.
Huldah speaks.
Judgment is real.
Sin is real.
But somewhere inside the palace, a king's heart is breaking before God.
And heaven notices.
Thousands of years later, the question is no longer what Josiah will do.
It is what you will do when the Word finds you.
Will you defend the idol?
Or destroy it?
Will you hide the wound?
Or bring it to Christ?
Will you explain away your sin?
Or confess it?
Will you merely admire Josiah's tender heart?
Or ask God for one?
The King who ultimately matters is not Josiah.
His name is Jesus.
And when Jesus rewrites a life, He does not merely improve the old story.
He makes the sinner His own.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
He teaches rebels to become disciples.
He takes people whose stories should have ended in darkness and makes their lives testimonies to undeserved grace.
And comment.
Don't disappear silently if God has put His finger on something.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Whatever is true.
Because maybe the most important thing Huldah's story teaches us is not merely that God can place His message in an unexpected messenger.
It is that when God finally puts His finger on the chapter we desperately wanted to hide, He is not asking us to rewrite it ourselves.
He is calling us to surrender the pen to Christ.
The Word may expose the scandal—but in the hands of Jesus, the scandal does not have to become the final sentence.
